# Assignment 02 — Application 1: Diabetes Prediction

**Student:** _<your name>_    **ID:** _<your id>_    **Class:** _<class>_
   **Date:** 2026-08-29

This notebook develops the diabetes-screening application from the raw survey file
through to a persisted model that the web and mobile services load without
modification. It is organised as the twenty-three sections of the assignment
notebook specification and follows the pipeline

```
Data → Understand → Clean → Represent → Learn → Evaluate → Persist → Deploy
```

Each computed result is followed by a short written interpretation.

## 0. Header and setup

The environment is fixed and recorded here so that the experiment can be reproduced.
A single constant, `RANDOM_SEED`, feeds every randomised step in the notebook, and
the versions of the main libraries are printed for the reproducibility section of the
report.

## 1. Problem definition

### 1.1 Real-world problem

Public-health programmes routinely need to screen a large adult population and decide
which individuals to refer for a confirmatory blood test or a lifestyle-intervention
programme. At the moment of screening no laboratory measurement is available; the
only information is a short self-reported health questionnaire. The United States
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) collects a questionnaire of exactly
this kind every year through the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS),
a national telephone survey. The application learns, from roughly 250,000 completed
questionnaires, a function that identifies the respondents most likely to already
have diabetes or pre-diabetes.

### 1.2 Supervised task

The task is binary **classification**. The input `X` is the vector of 21
questionnaire items for one respondent, listed in section 1.3. The target `y` is
`Diabetes_binary`, obtained from the three-level survey label `Diabetes_012` by
mapping "no diabetes" (0) to the negative class and both "pre-diabetes" (1) and
"diabetes" (2) to the positive class.

The two positive levels are combined because the screening decision they lead to is
the same — refer the respondent for follow-up — and because the pre-diabetes level on
its own accounts for only about 1.8% of the data, too few rows to support a reliable
third class.

### 1.3 Feature dictionary

The field meanings and codings below are taken from the UCI *CDC Diabetes Health
Indicators* dataset page
(https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/891/cdc+diabetes+health+indicators), which
documents this exact file. Every column is stored as `float64`, although all but
three are integer-coded categories.

| # | Feature | Type | Coding / units | Meaning (questionnaire item) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| — | `Diabetes_012` | target (raw) | 0 / 1 / 2 | 0 = no diabetes or gestational-only, 1 = pre-diabetes, 2 = diabetes. Collapsed to `Diabetes_binary` (0 vs {1,2}). |
| 1 | `HighBP` | binary | 0 / 1 | Ever told by a health professional that you have **high blood pressure**. |
| 2 | `HighChol` | binary | 0 / 1 | Ever told that your **blood cholesterol is high**. |
| 3 | `CholCheck` | binary | 0 / 1 | Had a **cholesterol check within the past 5 years**. |
| 4 | `BMI` | continuous | kg/m² (≈12–98 in data) | **Body-mass index**, computed by the CDC from self-reported height and weight. |
| 5 | `Smoker` | binary | 0 / 1 | Smoked **at least 100 cigarettes** in your entire life. |
| 6 | `Stroke` | binary | 0 / 1 | Ever told you **had a stroke**. |
| 7 | `HeartDiseaseorAttack` | binary | 0 / 1 | Ever had **coronary heart disease (CHD) or a myocardial infarction (MI)**. |
| 8 | `PhysActivity` | binary | 0 / 1 | Any **physical activity in the past 30 days** other than your regular job. |
| 9 | `Fruits` | binary | 0 / 1 | Eat **fruit ≥ 1 time per day**. |
| 10 | `Veggies` | binary | 0 / 1 | Eat **vegetables ≥ 1 time per day**. |
| 11 | `HvyAlcoholConsump` | binary | 0 / 1 | **Heavy drinker**: ≥ 14 drinks/week (men) or ≥ 7 drinks/week (women). |
| 12 | `AnyHealthcare` | binary | 0 / 1 | Have **any health-care coverage** (insurance, HMO, government plan, …). |
| 13 | `NoDocbcCost` | binary | 0 / 1 | In the past 12 months, **needed a doctor but could not afford one**. |
| 14 | `GenHlth` | ordinal | 1–5 | Self-rated general health: **1 = excellent, 2 = very good, 3 = good, 4 = fair, 5 = poor**. |
| 15 | `MentHlth` | count | 0–30 days | Number of days in the past 30 that **mental health was "not good"** (stress, depression, emotions). |
| 16 | `PhysHlth` | count | 0–30 days | Number of days in the past 30 that **physical health was "not good"** (illness or injury). |
| 17 | `DiffWalk` | binary | 0 / 1 | **Serious difficulty walking or climbing stairs**. |
| 18 | `Sex` | binary | 0 / 1 | **0 = female, 1 = male** (respondent's sex as recorded by BRFSS). |
| 19 | `Age` | ordinal | 1–13 bracket | 5-year **age band** (`_AGEG5YR`): 1 = 18–24, 2 = 25–29, 3 = 30–34, …, 9 = 60–64, …, 12 = 75–79, **13 = 80+**. |
| 20 | `Education` | ordinal | 1–6 | Highest schooling: 1 = none/kindergarten, 2 = grades 1–8, 3 = grades 9–11, 4 = high-school graduate/GED, 5 = some college / technical, 6 = **college graduate (4+ yrs)**. |
| 21 | `Income` | ordinal | 1–8 | Annual household income band: 1 = < \$10k, 2 = \$10–15k, 3 = \$15–20k, 4 = \$20–25k, 5 = \$25–35k, 6 = \$35–50k, 7 = \$50–75k, 8 = **≥ \$75k**. |

Four of the features — `GenHlth`, `Age`, `Education` and `Income` — are ordinal
codes whose numeric order matches their real order (a higher `GenHlth` is worse
health, a higher `Age` band is older, and so on). A single ordered numeric column
therefore preserves the information they carry, and section 10 confirms that each has
a monotonic relationship with diabetes risk. The dataset is entirely tabular; it
contains no free-text field, so the text-representation demonstration required
elsewhere in the assignment applies only to the e-commerce notebook.

## 2. Dataset source

The data is the **Diabetes Health Indicators Dataset**, file
`diabetes_012_health_indicators_BRFSS2015.csv`, published on Kaggle at
https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/alexteboul/diabetes-health-indicators-dataset and
mirrored as entry #891 of the UCI Machine Learning Repository
(https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/891/cdc+diabetes+health+indicators). Being
derived from a United States government survey it is in the public domain; the copy
used here was downloaded on 2026-08-29.

The file is a cleaned extract of the **CDC BRFSS 2015** telephone health survey. The
dataset author selected 21 indicators associated with diabetes and released three
variants; this is the three-class variant, in which `Diabetes_012` distinguishes no
diabetes, pre-diabetes and diabetes. All values are respondent self-reports; the CDC
groups several of them into bands (age into 13 bands, income into 8, general health
into 5), and rows where the respondent answered "don't know" or "refused" were
removed by the dataset author.

The raw file is stored at
`diabetes/data/diabetes_012_health_indicators_BRFSS2015.csv` — comma-separated, one
header row, all values `float64`. The number of observations and attributes is
reported in section 4, and the per-feature descriptions are the table in section 1.3.
## 3. Dataset loading

The file loads without error. The first column, `Diabetes_012`, is the survey label
and the remaining 21 columns are the questionnaire items described in section 1.3.
All values are already numeric, so no parsing or type conversion is needed at load
time. Each row corresponds to one adult respondent and holds every answer recorded
for that person.
## 4. Dataset inspection

The dataset has shape `(253680, 22)`: **253,680 observations**, one per respondent,
and **22 columns** — the 21 questionnaire features plus the `Diabetes_012` label.
Every column has dtype `float64` even though all but `BMI`, `MentHlth` and `PhysHlth`
are integer-coded categories.

`isna().sum()` returns zero for every column, so there are no explicitly missing
values. `duplicated().sum()` reports 23,899 rows (about 9.4%) that are exact copies
of another row; these are the subject of section 7. The summary statistics show two
ranges worth checking further: `BMI` runs from 12 to 98, and `MentHlth` and
`PhysHlth` sit at 0 for most respondents but extend to 30. The raw target is highly
imbalanced, with 213,703, 4,631 and 35,346 rows in classes 0, 1 and 2 respectively.
## 5. Data-quality analysis

The table summarises every quality issue found and the action planned for it. The
dataset is in good condition overall: there are no missing values, no free-text
columns, no identifier column and no type inconsistencies. Three matters need
attention.

The first is the block of exact duplicate rows, which is resolved in section 7.
Removing them shifts the positive rate from about 15.8% in the raw file to about
17.3%, because the duplicated rows are concentrated among the common "healthy"
answer profiles. The second is the extreme end of the `BMI` range, whose size and
nature are examined in section 9; all `BMI` values are ultimately retained. The
third is the class imbalance, which is addressed through stratified splitting,
class weighting and the choice of evaluation metric in sections 14, 17 and 19.

The right skew of `MentHlth` and `PhysHlth` is expected — both count "not good"
days out of the last 30 — and is treated as genuine data rather than as an anomaly.
## 6. Missing-value analysis

Every column has a missing count of zero, so no row is dropped and no column is
removed for sparsity, and there is no per-column imputation strategy to decide.

The numeric pipeline in section 15 nonetheless begins with a
`SimpleImputer(strategy="median")`. On this training data it does nothing, but it
means the deployed service can still respond when a real request omits a field: the
median value, learned only from the training split, is substituted. Keeping the
imputer in the pipeline also keeps the training-time and inference-time code paths
identical.
## 7. Duplicate analysis

The file has no respondent identifier, so the only duplicate that can be detected is
a row that repeats another row in full. There are 23,899 such rows, about 9.4% of the
data.

These rows are removed, and the removal happens before the train/validation/test
split. Two considerations lead to this. With 21 mostly-binary columns a proportion
of identical rows will arise by coincidence rather than from a respondent being
recorded twice, but the two cases cannot be told apart, and an identical answer
vector appearing in both the training and the test set would inflate the test score
through memorisation rather than generalisation — a form of data leakage. Removing
the duplicates also prevents the most common answer profiles from being given extra
weight during training. After the removal `N` is 229,781, and every later section
works from this de-duplicated frame.
## 8. Invalid-value analysis

Each domain check is a test that a column stays inside the range its coding allows.
All of the coded columns pass: the 14 binary columns contain only 0 and 1, `GenHlth`
lies in 1–5, `Age` in 1–13, `Education` in 1–6, `Income` in 1–8, and the two
"days" columns in 0–30.

`BMI` is the only column with values that fall outside a plausible domain. A small
number of rows record a `BMI` below 14 or above 80, which is barely compatible with
an adult able to answer a telephone survey, and a few hundred rows fall in the
60–80 band, which is unusual but corresponds to genuine severe obesity. No row is
altered or discarded at this stage; the magnitude of these values, and their effect,
are analysed in section 9, which concludes that all `BMI` values are kept.
## 9. Outlier analysis

The band table in 9a describes the shape of the `BMI` tail. Values below 14 make up
about 0.01% of the data. The 60–80 band is larger, around 0.25% of rows, and its
diabetes rate is at or above the population average, so these respondents behave like
genuine severe-obesity cases rather than recording errors; removing them would
discard real high-risk signal. The rows with `BMI` at or above 80, and those below
14, are the only physiologically doubtful ones, and they are too few to influence a
model fitted on roughly 230,000 rows.

Two features of the later modelling make the exact treatment of this tail immaterial.
The numeric block is standardised in the preprocessing pipeline, which keeps the
linear and distance-based models from being dominated by a few large values, and the
model carried through to deployment is tree-based, so it responds to the rank order
of `BMI` rather than to its magnitude — a value of 80 and a value of 98 fall on the
same side of every split. Appendix A reports a direct check of this: keeping,
clipping and dropping the extreme `BMI` rows all give the same validation metrics.

For `MentHlth` and `PhysHlth` the IQR rule flags the many respondents who report a
large number of "not good" days, up to the maximum of 30. That is a valid answer
rather than an error, so these columns are left as they are and `StandardScaler`
brings them onto a comparable scale. The de-duplication in section 7 is therefore the
only change made to the data.
## 10. Exploratory data analysis

Five figures are shown, using four plot types. Each is read as an observation of what
the figure shows, an interpretation of what it means, and its implication for the
model.

**Plot 1 — target class balance (bar chart).**
*Observation.* After de-duplication there are about 190,055 negative rows and about
39,726 positive rows.
*Interpretation.* Around 17.3% of respondents are positive; predicting the majority
class for everyone already reaches about 0.83 accuracy.
*Implication.* Accuracy is not an informative headline metric. The split is
stratified, the models use `class_weight="balanced"`, and F1, recall and ROC-AUC are
used for comparison.

**Plot 2 — BMI by class (violin plot).**
*Observation.* The positive class sits higher, with a median `BMI` near 31 against
about 27 for the negative class and a longer upper tail, but the two distributions
overlap heavily.
*Interpretation.* `BMI` carries a real, broadly monotonic signal but cannot separate
the classes on its own.
*Implication.* `BMI` is retained and standardised, and it is expected to rank among
the more important features without being decisive.

**Plot 3 — diabetes rate against age band (line plot).**
*Observation.* The positive rate rises steadily from about 2% in band 1 (ages 18–24)
to a plateau near 25% around bands 10–11 (ages 65–74), then falls back slightly for
the 80+ band.
*Interpretation.* Age is a strong ordinal risk factor that is close to linear over
most of its range.
*Implication.* `Age` can be supplied as a single ordinal numeric column; a linear
model captures most of the trend and a tree model can also represent the plateau and
the final dip.

**Plot 4 — diabetes rate against income band (horizontal bar chart).**
*Observation.* There is a clear negative gradient, from about 28% positive in the
lowest income band to about 11% in the highest.
*Interpretation.* Income acts as a proxy for diet, environment and access to care and
remains informative even though it is not a clinical measurement.
*Implication.* `Income` is kept as an ordinal numeric column. That part of the
model's behaviour reflects a socio-economic pattern, which is relevant to a fairness
discussion but not to the mechanics of the pipeline.

**Plot 5 — correlation matrix (heatmap).**
*Observation.* The features most correlated with `Diabetes_binary` are `GenHlth`
(r ≈ 0.28), `HighBP` (≈ 0.26), `BMI` (≈ 0.21), `DiffWalk` (≈ 0.21), `HighChol`
(≈ 0.20) and `Age` (≈ 0.19), while `Income`, `Education` and `PhysActivity` are the
strongest negative correlates. Among the features themselves the largest correlation
is `GenHlth`–`PhysHlth` (r ≈ 0.52), followed by `PhysHlth`–`DiffWalk` (≈ 0.47) and
`Income`–`Education` (≈ 0.42).
*Interpretation.* Several health-burden variables move together, but no pair is close
to collinear (all |r| < 0.6), so no column is redundant.
*Implication.* Linear models can be trained on the full feature set without removing
anything, and tree ensembles will spread importance across the correlated group. The
three strongest single correlates also define the small reference model used in
section 16.
## 11. Feature types

The 21 input features divide into 14 binary indicators, 4 ordinal codes and 3
continuous numerics. The single target is `Diabetes_binary`, derived from
`Diabetes_012`.

`Diabetes_012` is dropped from the feature set once the target has been built:
keeping it would let the model read the answer directly. The dataset contains no
identifier column, no text column and no constant column, so nothing else is
removed. The four ordinal codes are represented as single numeric columns for the
reasons given in sections 1.3 and 10.

## 12. Data representation

This section makes the link to Lecture 02 explicit. A tabular sample is a vector
$x = [x_1, \dots, x_d]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and the dataset is a matrix
$X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}$. The chain from file to model input is

```
CSV  ->  DataFrame  ->  clean feature matrix  ->  scaled matrix  ->  model input
```

The cell below prints one raw record together with the feature vector it becomes, and
reports the original DataFrame shape, the final `X` shape and its dtype. These are
the figures used in the report's data-representation summary.

`X` is the dense array passed to `model.fit(X, y)` and `model.predict(X)`. Its shape
is `(N, d)` with `d = 23`. The three continuous columns, the four ordinal codes and
the engineered day-count are median-imputed and then standardised to mean 0 and
standard deviation 1; the 14 binary indicators and the engineered `CardioRisk` flag
are already 0/1 and pass through unchanged. The array differs from the raw CSV in
three ways: `Diabetes_012` is removed, two engineered columns are added, and the
numeric block is scaled. No value is clipped and no row is dropped.

No one-hot encoding is used, because every input is numeric or ordinal. Scaling is
applied to the eight-column numeric block with `StandardScaler`, so that logistic
regression, the support-vector machine and k-nearest-neighbours are not dominated by
the wider raw range of `BMI`.
## 13. Feature engineering

Two features are added. `TotalUnhealthyDays` is the sum of `MentHlth` and `PhysHlth`,
capped at 60; it gives the model a single "total burden of poor-health days" value
that is steadier than either skewed column alone. `CardioRisk` is the logical OR of
`Stroke` and `HeartDiseaseorAttack`; each is rare on its own (about 4% and 9%), and
combining them produces one denser indicator of cardiovascular history.

No categorical encoding is required, since the dataset contains no nominal variable —
the four ordinal codes are already ordered and are kept numeric — and, following
section 9, `BMI` is neither clipped nor used to filter rows. The final feature
dimension is `d = 23`: the 21 raw features plus the two engineered ones. Because
`engineer()` is a stateless function, the deployed service reproduces both new
columns from the 21 raw inputs.
## 14. Train / validation / test split   $D = D_\text{train} \cup D_\text{val} \cup D_\text{test}$

The data is split into roughly 70% training, 15% validation and 15% test. The split
is stratified on the target, so each part keeps the overall positive rate of about
17.3%, and `random_state = 42` makes it reproducible.

Test data must not influence training or the fitting of any preprocessing step. If
the imputer or the scaler computed its median or its mean and standard deviation from
validation or test rows, the model would have indirect knowledge of those rows and
the reported score would be optimistic relative to genuinely new traffic. The
notebook avoids this in three ways: the exact duplicates were removed before the
split (section 7), so no answer vector is shared between the parts; the split is
performed before any call to `.fit()`; and every preprocessing step is fitted on
`X_train` alone and only applied to `X_val` and `X_test`.
## 15. Preprocessing pipeline

The preprocessing is a single `ColumnTransformer` with two branches. The numeric
branch imputes missing values with the training median and then standardises the
eight-column numeric block, so that the scale-sensitive models treat `BMI`, the
`Age` band and the day-counts on equal terms. The other branch passes the 15 binary
indicators through untouched, as they are already 0/1.

`make_preprocessor()` returns a fresh, unfitted object. Each model in section 17
receives its own copy, fitted on exactly the same training rows, and the copy that
belongs to the selected model is saved with it in section 22. The web, mobile and API
services load that fitted object and use it as-is; deployment never fits a new one.
## 16. Baseline models

Two reference points are established before the candidate models are trained, because
each answers a different question.

The first is a no-information baseline that always predicts the majority class. It
reaches about 0.83 accuracy while scoring 0 on both recall and F1: it never
identifies a single diabetic respondent. This makes concrete why accuracy is set
aside as the headline metric and why recall, F1 and ROC-AUC are used instead. Any
model that fails to beat this baseline on recall and F1 has learned nothing useful,
whatever its accuracy.

The second is a deliberately small model — an ordinary logistic regression using
only the three strongest correlates from section 10, `GenHlth`, `HighBP` and `BMI`.
It reaches a ROC-AUC of about 0.77. Beating a no-information baseline is trivial, so
this second reference sets the bar that the full-size models in section 17 must clear
by a worthwhile margin; if they cannot, the three-feature model would be the more
sensible thing to deploy.
## 17. Model training

Five models are trained: logistic regression, a decision tree, a random forest, an
RBF support-vector machine and k-nearest-neighbours.

The RBF support-vector machine does not train in acceptable time on the full
160,000-row training set, so a common subsample is used for the comparison itself.
Training the models on different amounts of data would confound model quality with
training-set size, so every candidate is fitted on the same stratified 25,000-row
sample of the training split, with the same preprocessing. The model chosen from this
comparison is then refitted on the complete training set in section 19 before it is
evaluated on the held-out test set and persisted, so that the deployed model still
benefits from every available row. Section 18 includes a check that the ranking of
the chosen model does not change between the 25,000-row fit and the full-data fit.

All five models share the same 25,000-row training sample and the same preprocessing.
The hyperparameters are as follows.

| Model | Key hyperparameters |
|---|---|
| LogisticRegression | `max_iter=1000`, `class_weight="balanced"` |
| DecisionTree | `max_depth=6`, `min_samples_leaf=50`, `class_weight="balanced"` |
| RandomForest | `n_estimators=300`, `max_depth=12`, `min_samples_leaf=20`, `class_weight="balanced_subsample"` |
| SVM (RBF) | `C=1.0`, `gamma="scale"`, `probability=True`, `class_weight="balanced"` |
| KNN | `n_neighbors=45`, `weights="distance"` |
## 18. Model comparison

The first table ranks the five models on the validation set by ROC-AUC. The random
forest is first at about 0.81, a little ahead of logistic regression at about 0.80,
with the decision tree and the RBF support-vector machine close behind. All four
clear the 3-feature reference model from section 16 (about 0.77) by a useful margin,
which shows that the full feature set and the larger models earn their additional
cost. K-nearest-neighbours is the exception: its accuracy is high but its recall is
only about 0.10, because `KNeighborsClassifier` has no class-weighting option and on
imbalanced data its neighbourhoods are dominated by the majority class, so it drifts
toward predicting "no diabetes".

The second table addresses the use of a subsample for selection. Refitting the
leading model on the full training set changes its ROC-AUC and F1 only marginally and
raises its recall by a few points. The 25,000-row sample was therefore adequate for
ranking the models, and the full-data refit is what section 19 evaluates and what is
persisted for deployment.
## 19. Evaluation

The selected model is evaluated once, on the held-out test set, after being refitted
on the full training data.

In the confusion matrix the rows are the actual class and the columns are the
prediction. The top-left cell is respondents correctly cleared. The top-right cell is
respondents flagged who do not have diabetes; each one costs a single unnecessary
confirmatory test, and there are many of them because the model is tuned toward
recall. The bottom-left cell is the serious error: respondents who do have diabetes
or pre-diabetes but are predicted healthy and so are sent away undiagnosed. The
bottom-right cell is the cases correctly identified and referred.

For a population screen the cost of a false negative — a missed, untreated case — is
much greater than the cost of a false positive, which is one extra blood test, so
**recall on the positive class is the metric that matters most**. On the test set the
model reaches a recall of about 0.74 at a precision of about 0.36, with a ROC-AUC of
about 0.81 as the threshold-independent summary. Accuracy, at about 0.72, is not
treated as the headline figure: the no-information baseline in section 16 scored
higher on accuracy and was of no use.
## 20. Error analysis

Comparing the average feature values of the errors with the test set as a whole
explains where the model breaks down.

The false negatives resemble the healthy population on average: a near-average `BMI`,
a low (good) `GenHlth`, and fewer `HighBP` and `DiffWalk` flags. These are diabetics
whose risk comes from factors the questionnaire does not record — family history,
diet detail, a fasting glucose value — so the failure is a gap in the representation
rather than a lack of model capacity. The false positives are the opposite: they
carry many risk markers, including high `BMI`, poor `GenHlth`, `HighBP` and
`HighChol`, but have not (yet) developed diabetes. These are the high-risk
non-cases that a screening model is expected to over-select.

The remedies follow from this. The representation gap could be closed by adding
features the survey lacks or by obtaining a single laboratory value; alternatively,
lowering the decision threshold would trade further precision for recall where
follow-up capacity allows.

## 21. Model selection

The model chosen for deployment is the **random forest**, the leading model in the
section 18 comparison. On the held-out test set it reaches a ROC-AUC of about 0.81, a
recall of about 0.74 and an F1 of about 0.48, and it stays clear of both baselines.

| Criterion | Random forest (deployed) | Logistic regression (fallback) |
|---|---|---|
| Predictive performance | best ROC-AUC and best F1 in section 18 | about 0.01 ROC-AUC behind — effectively equal |
| Interpretability | feature importances and per-tree paths | signed coefficients as odds ratios, more directly readable by clinicians |
| Computational cost | trains in a few seconds; under 10 ms per prediction | trains in under a second; under 1 ms per prediction |
| Artifact size | about 55 MB pickled (300 trees) | about 30 KB pickled |
| Robustness | bagging absorbs noise and outliers, models feature interactions directly, and is insensitive to the `BMI` tail (section 9) | linear decision surface; depends on the pipeline's scaler |
| Deployment constraints | CPU-only, no dependency beyond scikit-learn | CPU-only, very small |

The random forest is preferred because it is the strongest model on both headline
metrics and adds no operational difficulty: the artifact is large but loads in well
under a second and serves single requests in a few milliseconds, which is acceptable
for a screening API. Logistic regression is retained as a documented fallback — if
artifact size or coefficient-level interpretability later becomes a hard requirement,
it can replace the random forest for a cost of about 0.01 ROC-AUC by changing one
line in section 22. The support-vector machine and k-nearest-neighbours are not
considered for deployment: both were fitted only on the 25,000-row sample, k-nearest
-neighbours would have to carry the training data inside the artifact and reached a
recall of only about 0.10, and the RBF support-vector machine has the slowest
inference of the five.
## 22. Model persistence

For deployment the pipeline is refitted once more, on the training and validation
data together — every row except the held-out test set — so that it uses as much data
as possible. The preprocessing is refitted on the same combined data, which keeps the
test set outside the fit.

Three files are written to `diabetes/model/`. `model_pipeline.joblib` is a single
object containing the fitted imputer and scaler and the random forest.
`feature_names.joblib` is the ordered list of 23 feature names that the API must
build before calling the pipeline. `input_schema.json` is a human-readable contract
listing the 21 raw fields, the 2 engineered fields, the valid range of each, the
chosen model, the random seed and the scikit-learn version. Nothing further is needed
at inference: the API loads `model_pipeline.joblib`, rebuilds the feature frame with
the same `engineer()` function, and calls `predict_proba`.
## 23. Inference test

This section runs the contract that the web and mobile services depend on. The
pipeline is reloaded from disk as fresh objects, a single raw 21-field dictionary —
the same shape a client will POST — is passed through field validation, the
`engineer()` function and the loaded pipeline, and the result is returned as

```json
{ "prediction": "diabetic", "confidence": 0.85 }
```

No scaler, imputer or model is fitted here. The assertion confirms that the artifact
loaded from disk produces exactly the same probability as the in-memory pipeline from
section 22, so the path `raw input → validation → engineer() → fitted preprocessing →
model → prediction` is reproducible outside the notebook.

---

## Appendix A — Sensitivity check on BMI-outlier handling

Section 9 keeps every `BMI` value unchanged. This appendix quantifies the claim made
there — that the treatment of the extreme values does not affect model quality — and
checks that the choice is safe even if some of the extreme-`BMI` respondents are
genuine. It is kept separate from section 9 because it requires fitting models.

On a fresh stratified split of 60,000 training rows and 20,000 held-out rows from the
de-duplicated data, a logistic regression and a random forest are fitted under four
`BMI` policies — keep all values, clip to [12, 80], clip to [14, 60], and drop the
rows outside [14, 80] — and compared on ROC-AUC, F1 and recall.

Across the four policies the metrics vary by no more than about 0.003 in ROC-AUC and
0.003 in F1 for either model, which is within run-to-run noise. There are two
reasons. The extreme-`BMI` rows are a very small fraction of roughly 230,000
observations, so they carry almost no weight in the fitted parameters under any
policy; and the deployed model is a random forest, which splits on rank order, so a
value of 80 and a value of 98 lie on the same side of every threshold and clipping
has no effect on it.

Keeping the values is therefore the safe choice. If some of the extreme-`BMI`
respondents are genuine — and the elevated diabetes rate of the 60–80 band in section
9 suggests they are — nothing is lost by keeping them, and if a few are coding errors
they are too rare to matter. No clipping is applied in the pipeline.
